quote: Was ist der entsprechende, wenn mehrere lineare Transforma- tionen gegeben sind, wie z. B. wenn man die Coefficienten einer binären Form betrachtet und [-diese-] die in dieser auftretenden Coefficienten linear transformirt?
english: What is the corresponding thing when several linear transformations are given, as for example when one considers the coefficients of a binary form and transforms the coefficients occurring in it linearly?
topic: Hilbert asks what the analogue is when several linear transformations are given, such as when the coefficients of a binary form are transformed linearly, and begins (then crosses out) an approach using invariants and power-series expansions of nearby value systems in parameters.

triage.modern_statement: The note can only be partly reconstructed. 'Das Entsprechende' refers to some object or result from the preceding text that this note does not name. A plausible modern reading: given a group generated by several linear transformations, or the action of GL2/SL2 on the coefficient space of binary forms of degree n (the representation Sym^n of C^2), what plays the role, for the whole group, of the object previously studied for a single linear transformation? The crossed-out approach mentions invariants and power-series expansions of nearby value systems in parameters. That would fit a local or infinitesimal study of the invariants of this action. But the object being generalized is not stated, so the exact question cannot be fixed.
triage.answered_by: No specific answer can be assigned. If the question is read as asking for the invariants of the induced linear action on the coefficients of binary forms, it belongs to classical invariant theory. Gordan proved finite generation for binary forms in 1868 and for systems of binary forms in 1870. Hilbert gave a general nonconstructive finiteness proof in 1890 (Math. Ann.). The general question of finite generation for arbitrary linear group actions became Hilbert's 14th problem, which Nagata answered in the negative in the late 1950s.

evidence.claim: Gordan proved the first fundamental theorem for invariants of binary forms in 1868 and for systems of binary forms in 1870. Hilbert gave a general nonconstructive proof for any system of forms in 1890.
Invariants of the coefficients of binary forms, generalized to more variables and several forms, was the classical setting of Hilbert's finiteness theorem.
Nagata gave the first counterexamples to Hilbert's 14th problem (finite generation of invariant rings for general linear group actions) in the late 1950s, and further counterexamples followed.
Hilbert's 14th problem and Zariski's reformulation of it.

triage.why: The note asks for 'the corresponding thing' for several transformations, but this page does not say what that thing is for a single transformation, and the approach that would clarify it is crossed out. The setting (linear transformations induced on the coefficients of binary forms) is clearly classical invariant theory, which Gordan and Hilbert largely settled and which led to Hilbert's 14th problem. Still, no source ties this particular diary entry to a specific later result. Treating it as solved or as one of the published problems would go beyond what the sources support.
